extracted.intended_audience: federal appellate judges, district court judges, patent litigators, patent prosecutors, USPTO examiners, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for construing patent claim terms (how courts should weigh intrinsic and extrinsic evidence, avoid importing limitations, treat dictionaries, apply doctrines like claim differentiation, and the proper degree of appellate deference). Aimed at informing judicial and practitioner approaches to claim construction disputes on appeal and at trial/prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance public notice and fair scope of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction should balance the public notice function of patents with the competing policy of a fair scope of protection for patentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations should facilitate equitable treatment of patentees and the public and produce predictability; courts should ensure patentees 'understand, and correctly describe, just what he has invented, and for what he claims a patent' (Merrill v. Yeomans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is a legal question reviewed de novo
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim interpretation is a matter of law (Markman; Cybor) and is reviewed de novo on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although legal and reviewed de novo, courts should recognize that certain aspects (e.g., local findings based on live testimony) may merit deference or greater weight; see Cybor concurrences/dissents and the Ornelas analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence (Vitronics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence of record — the claims, specification, prosecution history and cited prior art — is the primary source for claim meaning and should be given primacy over extrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is 'usually dispositive; it is the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term.' Rely on intrinsic evidence first to preserve doctrines of patent law and settled expectations (Vitronics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence only to resolve remaining ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, treatises, dictionaries) may be used only when intrinsic evidence leaves ambiguity and may not be used to contradict intrinsic evidence or vary the scope of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If intrinsic evidence provides sufficient clarity, reliance on extrinsic evidence is improper; extrinsic evidence may 'help the court come to the proper understanding of the claim term' but cannot trump intrinsic sources (Vitronics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries and treatises are objective but not presumptive baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries and treatises are relatively objective extrinsic aids, but they should not establish a presumptive baseline meaning that displaces intrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Texas Digital advocated starting with dictionaries and giving them a 'heavy presumption', the government view here is that dictionaries should elucidate intrinsic evidence rather than serve as the initial baseline; avoid a 'battle of the dictionaries' and the unpredictability of selecting among different dictionaries or definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may define terms explicitly or implicitly (lexicography/by implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification can define a term expressly (lexicography) or 'define [them] by implication' through consistent usage throughout the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit definitions or consistent usage across the specification to determine whether the specification sets the appropriate meaning (Novartis, Vanderlande, Bell Atlantic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret terms from perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be construed from the viewpoint of one of ordinary skill in the art; judges should attempt to replicate that perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extrinsic evidence when necessary to ascertain the level of ordinary skill and the art-recognized meaning of technical terms; for non-technical words a dictionary may be unnecessary (Brookhill-Wilk; Microsoft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence must elucidate intrinsic evidence, not supplant it
rubrics_metrics.description: When used, extrinsic materials should illuminate and help interpret the intrinsic record, not replace or contradict it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult extrinsic sources only to aid understanding of the intrinsic evidence; resist relying on extrinsic sources 'in a vacuum' because each source influences the understanding of one skilled in the art (Markman; Alloc; Vanderlande).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing limitations from the specification into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must avoid impermissibly reading embodiments, exemplary features, or specification-only details into the claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe claims to include features that appear only in exemplary embodiments or to satisfy best-mode disclosure unless the specification as a whole demonstrates that the feature is essential to every embodiment or used to characterize the invention (Markman; Tate; Alloc; Sumace Roots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize whether a specification feature is exemplary or essential
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether to import a specification feature into a claim, determine if a person of ordinary skill would view the feature as merely exemplary or essential to the invention's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification 'as a whole suggests that the very character of the invention requires the limitation be a part of every embodiment,' then importing may be appropriate; if merely exemplary or used only for best mode, do not import (Alloc; Sumace Roots; SciMed; Wang Labs; Toro).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claim differentiation only as an aid when ambiguity persists
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim differentiation (not reading a limitation into a claim that appears in another claim) is a proper secondary tool where intrinsic/extrinsic evidence fail to yield a single clear definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply claim differentiation sparingly to avoid overshadowing the express intentions of the draftsman; reserved for when review of intrinsic/extrinsic evidence fails to produce a single meaning (SRI Int'l; Hormone Research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrict interpretation to preserve validity when multiple reasonable meanings exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When several reasonable interpretations exist and one would render the claim invalid, construe claims, where practicable, to preserve validity consistent with 35 U.S.C. § 282.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine is limited: the preserving-construction must be practicable, based on sound claim-construction principles, and must not revise or ignore explicit claim language (Liebel-Flarsheim; Generation II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrict ambiguous coinages against the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disputed term lacks a customary meaning and was essentially created by the patentee (and not defined in the specification/prosecution history), construe it narrowly against the drafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the patentee failed to fulfill the obligation to define the term, meaning should be derived from the patent context and be narrow to serve notice (J.T. Eaton; Athletic Alternatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prosecution history and USPTO context
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history and the manner in which the USPTO examined/understood the claims are relevant intrinsic considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the USPTO gives claims their 'broadest reasonable interpretation' during prosecution, courts should consult intrinsic evidence (specification, cited prior art, prosecution arguments) to avoid interpretations at odds with the USPTO's understanding (In re Morris; In re American Academy of Sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of dictionary multiplicity and sequential-definition chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequentially dissecting terms via multiple dictionaries or using different dictionaries across cases generates unpredictability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid approaches that break a term into component words and define each through separate dictionary lookups or that rely on inconsistent choice among dictionaries (examples: Novartis/Eon Labs, Nvstrom, Int'l Rectifier, TI Group, Anchor Wall). Such practices undermine predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the patent as a fully integrated written instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent should be read as an integrated whole; terms must be defined in a way that comports with the instrument as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction is a 'necessarily sophisticated analysis of the whole [patent] document' and a term's meaning must align with the document in its entirety (Markman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review: give due weight to persuasive district court constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although review is de novo, appellate courts should give due consideration to district court constructions that are persuasive, especially where the district court had the benefit of live testimony or a fuller record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an approach analogous to Ornelas/International Trade Court review: do not start from a 'clean slate' — give weight to the care shown in the record and the district court's informed opinions, while retaining ultimate de novo review (Cybor concurrences, ALTX, Ornelas).
